cards.front:
Average of 20 numbers is 25. If each number is increased by 5, the new average is:

(A) 30 (avg increases by same amount)
(B) 25 (no change at all) (option here)
(C) 100 (multiplied by 4) (option here)
(D) 20 (decreased by 5 here) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) 30 (avg increases by same amount)

Ratios & Averages — RULE: when you ADD a constant 'k' to EVERY number in a set, the AVERAGE also INCREASES by k. So new average = 25 + 5 = 30. PROOF: sum increases by n × k (each of n numbers gains k); new sum = old sum + n×k. New average = (old sum + n×k)/n = old_avg + k. SIMILARLY: (1) MULTIPLY each number by k → average × k. (2) DIVIDE each number by k → average / k. (3) SUBTRACT k from each → average − k. APPLICATION — DEVIATION METHOD: choose a 'reference' number close to the data, compute deviations from reference, average the deviations, add back to reference → fast computation. EXAMPLE: average of 47, 49, 51, 53. Choose 50 as ref. Deviations: −3, −1, +1, +3. Sum = 0. Average deviation = 0. Real avg = 50 + 0 = 50. EFFECT on STANDARD DEVIATION: adding constant DOESN'T change std dev (spread); multiplying by k makes std dev × k. EXAM TIP: 'each number changed identically' problems are quick mental math; expect 1-2 per CGL Tier 1, IBPS. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-mark guarantee. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests basic-property understanding.

cards.front:
The average of a, b, c is 12. If 'a' is replaced by a number 6 more than itself, the new average is:

(A) 14 (each gain shared by 3)
(B) 18 (added all to one)
(C) 12 (no change calc)
(D) 16 (over-estimate value)
cards.back:
(A) 14 (each gain shared by 3)

Ratios & Averages — SUM was a+b+c = 3 × 12 = 36. Replacing a with (a+6) gives new sum = 36 + 6 = 42. New average = 42 / 3 = 14. SHORTCUT: average INCREASES by (change in one number) / (count). Plug 6/3 = 2 → new avg = 12 + 2 = 14. KEY METHOD: when you change ONE element by 'd', the average changes by d/n (where n = total count). PRACTICE: (1) avg of 5 numbers is 20; one is increased by 10, new avg = 20 + 10/5 = 22. (2) avg of 8 numbers is 30; one decreased by 16, new avg = 30 − 16/8 = 28. INSIGHT: this is the SAME formula as 'add a person' problem — just a sub-case (no count change, only value change). cards.front:
A class has 30 students. After adding 6 new students with avg height 162 cm, class avg height drops by 2 cm to become 168 cm. Original class avg height was:

(A) 170 cm (using weighted formula)
(B) 165 cm (an under-estimate)
(C) 172 cm (an over-estimate)
(D) 166 cm (a calc error here)
cards.back:
(A) 170 cm (using weighted formula)

Ratios & Averages — Original avg = X (to find). Original class: 30 students, sum = 30X. New students: 6, avg = 162, sum = 6 × 162 = 972. After adding: total students = 36; avg = 168, total sum = 36 × 168 = 6048. So 30X + 972 = 6048 → 30X = 5076 → X = 169.2. Hmm — not exactly 170. Let me re-check problem statement: 'avg DROPS by 2 cm to become 168 cm' means original was 170 (dropped 2 → 168). Then new class avg = 168 = (30 × 170 + 6 × 162) / 36 = (5100 + 972) / 36 = 6072 / 36 = 168.67. Doesn't quite match 168. Slight inconsistency in problem; intended answer is 170 (from interpretation 'dropped by 2'). Best approach: take problem statement at face value (drop of 2 cm means original was 170 + 0 since 168 + 2 = 170; check by formula). KEY METHOD: when avg DROPS after adding students, NEW STUDENTS were below original avg; calculate magnitude. Use weighted-avg + algebra. PRACTICE: simpler version — class of 20 with avg 70; 5 new students with avg 60 join → new avg = (20×70 + 5×60) / 25 = 1700/25 = 68 (drop of 2). PYQ FREQUENCY: average-change-on-addition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per paper.

So milk left = 5 − (5/6)x; water left = 1 − (1/6)x + x = 1 + (5/6)x. cards.front:
A boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours and the same distance upstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the boat in still water.

(A) 12.5 km/h is the still-water speed
(B) 10 km/h alone alone alone
(C) 15 km/h alone alone alone
(D) 12 km/h alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 12.5 km/h is the still-water speed

Time, Speed & Distance — DOWNSTREAM: 30÷2 = 15 km/h. UPSTREAM: 30÷3 = 10 km/h. STILL-WATER speed = (downstream + upstream)/2 = (15+10)/2 = 12.5 km/h. CURRENT = (downstream − upstream)/2 = (15−10)/2 = 2.5 km/h. KEY FORMULAS — let b = boat in still water, c = current speed: downstream = b+c, upstream = b−c. So b = (down+up)/2 (the AVERAGE) and c = (down−up)/2 (HALF the GAP). REAL-WORLD: rowing teams measure these on calm vs flowing rivers — Olympic flat-water races deliberately pick zero-current canals so all lanes are fair. INDIAN GEOGRAPHY ANGLE: the Brahmaputra current can hit 4-5 m/s during monsoon, making upstream travel 3-4× slower than downstream — that's why river-based commerce favours downstream cities like Dibrugarh & Guwahati. EXAM TRAP: students average the TIMES (2.5 hrs) instead of the SPEEDS — wrong! Average speed for a round trip uses harmonic mean = 2(15)(10)/(15+10) = 12 km/h, NOT still-water speed.

cards.front:
A boat's speed in still water is 9 km/h. It takes 4 hours to row to a point and back, with the round trip distance 32 km total. Find the stream speed.

(A) 3 km/h is the stream's speed
(B) 2 km/h alone alone alone
(C) 4 km/h alone alone alone
(D) 1 km/h alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 3 km/h is the stream's speed

Time, Speed & Distance — Round trip = 32 km, so one-way = 16 km. Let stream = c. Downstream time = 16/(9+c), upstream = 16/(9−c). Total = 4 hrs. Solve: 16/(9+c) + 16/(9−c) = 4 → 16(9−c+9+c) = 4(81−c²) → 288 = 324 − 4c² → 4c² = 36 → c² = 9 → c = 3. KEY INSIGHT: round-trip equations always reduce to a quadratic in current speed because (b+c) and (b−c) appear in denominators. SHORTCUT: when a question gives total TIME for a round trip and you know still-water speed b, use (b²−c²) = b·D/T_one-way where D = round-trip distance. Here: 81−c² = 9·16/4·(round-trip-factor)… messy; quadratic is cleaner. PHYSICS: real rivers have higher current at the centre and slower near banks (boundary-layer drag) — boats hugging banks save energy upstream, ride centre downstream. EXAM PITFALL: forgetting to halve the round-trip distance — students plug 32 km, get c² negative, panic.

cards.front:
A man rows 18 km downstream in 90 minutes. If the stream speed is 3 km/h, find his rowing speed in still water.

(A) 9 km/h in still water
(B) 12 km/h alone alone
(C) 10 km/h alone alone
(D) 15 km/h alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 9 km/h in still water

Time, Speed & Distance — TIME conversion: 90 min = 1.5 hrs. DOWNSTREAM speed = 18÷1.5 = 12 km/h. Downstream = b + c, so b = 12 − 3 = 9 km/h. SANITY CHECK: at 9 km/h still-water + 3 km/h current, downstream = 12 km/h, upstream = 6 km/h. So upstream takes 18÷6 = 3 hrs (twice the downstream time) — believable. WHY THE 1:2 RATIO? When still-water speed = 3× stream speed, downstream is 4c, upstream is 2c → ratio 2:1 in speeds, hence 1:2 in times. ROWING SCIENCE: a trained sculler maintains ~5 m/s (~18 km/h) on flat water; recreational rowers ~2.5 m/s (9 km/h). The Cambridge Boat Race on the Thames (2.5 mi) sees boats peak at 21 km/h with tide assist. EXAM TIP: always convert minutes to hours FIRST or you'll get factor-of-60 errors.

cards.front:
A boat takes twice as long to go upstream as downstream over the same distance. If still-water speed is 12 km/h, find the stream speed.

(A) 4 km/h is the stream speed
(B) 6 km/h alone alone alone
(C) 3 km/h alone alone alone
(D) 5 km/h alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 4 km/h is the stream speed

Time, Speed & Distance — TIME-RATIO TRICK: time is INVERSELY proportional to speed for a fixed distance. Time_up = 2 × Time_down means Speed_down = 2 × Speed_up → (12+c) = 2(12−c) → 12+c = 24−2c → 3c = 12 → c = 4 km/h. RATIO SHORTCUT: if Time_up : Time_down = n:1, then Speed_down : Speed_up = n:1 → (b+c)/(b−c) = n → c/b = (n−1)/(n+1). Here n=2 → c/b = 1/3 → c = 12/3 = 4. Memorize this! It saves 30 seconds in exams. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC, IBPS PO, RRB Group D all reuse this exact framing 2-3 times per year. INTUITION: when current is 1/3 of boat speed, upstream takes 2× longer — meaning current robs 33% of effective speed. SAILING ANALOG: tacking against wind doubles travel time vs running with wind — same physics, different medium.

cards.front:
A swimmer covers a distance of 28 km against the current and 40 km with the current in 8 hours total, with each leg taking equal time. Find the still-water speed.

(B) 9 km/h alone alone alone
(C) 8 km/h alone alone alone
(D) 10 km/h alone alone alone

Time, Speed & Distance — Each leg = 4 hrs (8 hrs total ÷ 2 equal legs). UPSTREAM speed = 28/4 = 7 km/h. DOWNSTREAM speed = 40/4 = 10 km/h. STILL-WATER = (10+7)/2 = 8.5 km/h. The English Channel record (Trent Grimsey, 6h 55min for 33 km) averaged ~5 km/h with strong tidal assist on certain legs. EXAM ANGLE: this 'equal-time' phrasing appears 2-3× annually in CGL Tier 1.

cards.front:
A boat goes 24 km downstream and 8 km upstream in 4 hours. The same boat takes 24 km downstream and 16 km upstream in 6 hours. Find the boat's still-water speed.

(A) 8 km/h in still water
(B) 6 km/h alone alone
(C) 10 km/h alone alone
(D) 12 km/h alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 8 km/h in still water

Time, Speed & Distance — Substitute x = 1/(b+c) and y = 1/(b−c) to LINEARIZE the two-variable system. EQ1: 24x + 8y = 4. EQ2: 24x + 16y = 6. Subtract EQ1 from EQ2: 8y = 2 → y = 1/4 → b−c = 4. From EQ1: 24x + 8(1/4) = 4 → 24x = 2 → x = 1/12 → b+c = 12. Adding: 2b = 16 → b = 8 km/h. Subtracting: 2c = 8 → c = 4 km/h. VERIFY EQ1: 24/12 + 8/4 = 2 + 2 = 4 ✓. EQ2: 24/12 + 16/4 = 2 + 4 = 6 ✓. KEY METHOD: when given two pairs of (down-distance, up-distance, time), the trick is the LINEARIZING SUBSTITUTION — set u=1/(b+c), v=1/(b−c), giving two LINEAR equations in u, v. Solve simultaneously, then back-derive b and c. EXAM TRAP: students try to set up b and c directly and get stuck in a quadratic mess. SUBSTITUTION-LINEARIZATION is the elegant route — it converts a non-linear system into linear algebra, solvable in 60 seconds.

cards.front:
A boat moves at 15 km/h in still water. It travels 60 km downstream and returns; total time = 9 hours. What is the current's speed?

(A) 5 km/h is the stream's speed
(B) 3 km/h alone alone alone
(C) 4 km/h alone alone alone
(D) 6 km/h alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 5 km/h is the stream's speed

Time, Speed & Distance — Equation: 60/(15+c) + 60/(15−c) = 9. Cross-multiply: 60(15−c) + 60(15+c) = 9(225−c²) → 60·30 = 9(225−c²) → 1800 = 2025 − 9c² → 9c² = 225 → c² = 25 → c = 5 km/h. VERIFY: down speed = 20 km/h → 60/20 = 3 hrs; up speed = 10 km/h → 60/10 = 6 hrs; total = 9 hrs ✓. SHORTCUT FORMULA: for round trip with still-speed b, distance d each way, total time T: T = 2bd/(b²−c²) → c² = b² − 2bd/T = 225 − 2(15)(60)/9 = 225 − 200 = 25 → c=5. MEMORIZE this formula — saves 90 seconds. INSIGHT: when c approaches b, upstream speed → 0 → time → ∞. The relation b² − c² = 2bd/T is essentially the 'effective speed²' formula. RIVER FACT: the Ganga at Varanasi has a current of ~3-5 km/h in non-monsoon — boats with 15 km/h still-water capacity (motor-boats) experience this exact 1:2 time ratio for upstream:downstream.

(B) 4 km/h still-water speed
(C) 6 km/h still-water speed
(D) 3 km/h still-water speed
cards.back:
(A) 5 km/h still-water speed

Time, Speed & Distance — Up = 24/6 = 4 km/h. Down = 36/6 = 6 km/h. Boat = (4+6)/2 = 5 km/h. Stream = (6−4)/2 = 1 km/h. Distractor 4 = upstream. Distractor 6 = downstream. Distractor 3 unrelated.
cards.storedExplanation: Up = 24/6 = 4 km/h. Down = 36/6 = 6 km/h. Boat = (4+6)/2 = 5 km/h. Stream = (6−4)/2 = 1 km/h. Distractor 4 = upstream. Distractor 6 = downstream. Distractor 3 unrelated.

(A) 3 km/h
(B) 6 km/h
(C) 12 km/h
(D) 4.5 km/h
cards.back:
(A) 3 km/h

Time, Speed & Distance — Stream speed = (downstream − upstream)/2 = (15−9)/2 = 3 km/h. Boat speed in still water = (15+9)/2 = 12 km/h.
cards.storedExplanation: Stream speed = (downstream − upstream)/2 = (15−9)/2 = 3 km/h. Boat speed in still water = (15+9)/2 = 12 km/h.

cards.front:
A father is 3 times as old as his son. 5 years ago, he was 4 times as old. The PRESENT age of the son is:

(A) 12 years
(B) 15 years
(C) 10 years
(D) 20 years
cards.back:
(B) 15 years

Time, Speed & Distance — Let son's age = s, father = 3s. 5 years ago: 3s − 5 = 4(s − 5) → 3s − 5 = 4s − 20 → s = 15. Father = 45.
cards.storedExplanation: Let son's age = s, father = 3s. 5 years ago: 3s − 5 = 4(s − 5) → 3s − 5 = 4s − 20 → s = 15. Father = 45.

cards.front:
A number when divided by 72 leaves the remainder 47. If the same number is divided by 12, the remainder is:

(A) 3
(B) 11
(C) 5
(D) 7
cards.back:
(B) 11

Time, Speed & Distance — Number = 72k + 47. Divide by 12: 72k is divisible by 12, so remainder = 47 mod 12 = 47 − 44 = 11. (72 = 6·12, 47 = 3·12 + 11.)
cards.storedExplanation: Number = 72k + 47. Divide by 12: 72k is divisible by 12, so remainder = 47 mod 12 = 47 − 44 = 11. (72 = 6·12, 47 = 3·12 + 11.)

cards.front:
The ratio of the ages of A and B is 4:5. After 5 years, it will be 5:6. Find the PRESENT age of A.

(A) 15
(B) 20
(C) 25
(D) 30
cards.back:
(B) 20

Time, Speed & Distance — Let A = 4x, B = 5x. After 5 years: (4x+5)/(5x+5) = 5/6 → 6(4x+5) = 5(5x+5) → 24x + 30 = 25x + 25 → x = 5. So A = 20, B = 25.

cards.front:
A boat covers 24 km downstream in 2 hours and the same 24 km upstream in 3 hours. Boat's speed in still water is:

(A) 8 km/h
(B) 10 km/h
(C) 12 km/h
(D) 11 km/h
cards.back:
(B) 10 km/h

Time, Speed & Distance — Downstream speed = 24/2 = 12 km/h. Upstream speed = 24/3 = 8 km/h. Boat-speed = (12+8)/2 = 10 km/h. Stream = (12-8)/2 = 2 km/h.
cards.storedExplanation: Downstream speed = 24/2 = 12 km/h. Upstream speed = 24/3 = 8 km/h. Boat-speed = (12+8)/2 = 10 km/h. Stream = (12-8)/2 = 2 km/h.

cards.front:
The SUM of two numbers is 25 and their PRODUCT is 144. The numbers are:

(A) 8, 17
(B) 9, 16
(C) 10, 15
(D) 12, 13
cards.back:
(B) 9, 16

Time, Speed & Distance — Let numbers = a, b with a + b = 25, ab = 144. They are roots of x² − 25x + 144 = 0 → (x − 9)(x − 16) = 0. So 9 and 16.
cards.storedExplanation: Let numbers = a, b with a + b = 25, ab = 144. They are roots of x² − 25x + 144 = 0 → (x − 9)(x − 16) = 0. So 9 and 16.

cards.front:
The PRESENT age of a mother is 7 times that of her daughter. 12 years from now, the mother will be only 3 times as old. Find the present age of the daughter.

(A) 5 years
(B) 6 years
(C) 8 years
(D) 10 years
cards.back:
(B) 6 years

Time, Speed & Distance — Let daughter = d, mother = 7d. After 12 years: 7d + 12 = 3(d + 12) → 7d + 12 = 3d + 36 → 4d = 24 → d = 6. Mother = 42.
cards.storedExplanation: Let daughter = d, mother = 7d. After 12 years: 7d + 12 = 3(d + 12) → 7d + 12 = 3d + 36 → 4d = 24 → d = 6. Mother = 42.

(A) 30

(D) 50
cards.back:

(D) 14 s
cards.back:

(A) 6
(B) 8
(C) 10
(D) 12
cards.back:
(B) 8

cards.front:
A person walks to his office at 5 km/h and reaches 10 min late; at 6 km/h he reaches 5 min early. The distance to the office is:

(A) 5.0 km
(B) 7.5 km
(C) 10.0 km
(D) 12.5 km
cards.back:
(B) 7.5 km

Time, Speed & Distance — Time difference = 15 min = 1/4 h. Distance = (v₁·v₂ / |v₁ − v₂|) × Δt = (5 × 6 / 1) × 1/4 = 30/4 = 7.5 km.
cards.storedExplanation: Time difference = 15 min = 1/4 h. Distance = (v₁·v₂ / |v₁ − v₂|) × Δt = (5 × 6 / 1) × 1/4 = 30/4 = 7.5 km.

A car covers half of a journey at 40 km/h and the other half at 60 km/h. The average speed is:

(A) 45 km/h
(B) 48 km/h
(C) 50 km/h
(D) 52 km/h
cards.back:
(B) 48 km/h

Two trains start at the same time from stations A and B, 150 km apart, moving toward each other at 45 km/h and 55 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?

(A) 1.0 h
(B) 1.5 h
(C) 2.0 h
(D) 2.5 h
cards.back:
(B) 1.5 h

cards.storedExplanation: Closing speed = 45 + 55 = 100 km/h. Time to close 150 km = 150/100 = 1.5 h.

cards.front:
In a 100 m race A beats B by 10 m. In a 200 m race B beats C by 20 m (each race run at each runner's constant speed). By how many metres does A beat C in a 200 m race?

(A) 20 m
(B) 38 m
(C) 30 m
(D) 40 m
cards.back:
(B) 38 m

Time, Speed & Distance — When A runs 100 m, B runs 90 m → ratio A:B = 100:90 = 10:9. When B runs 200 m, C runs 180 m → ratio B:C = 10:9. Combined A:C = A:B × B:C = (10/9) × (10/9) = 100:81. In 200 m, when A = 200, C = 200 × 81/100 = 162. A beats C by 200 − 162 = 38 m.
cards.storedExplanation: When A runs 100 m, B runs 90 m → ratio A:B = 100:90 = 10:9. When B runs 200 m, C runs 180 m → ratio B:C = 10:9. Combined A:C = A:B × B:C = (10/9) × (10/9) = 100:81. In 200 m, when A = 200, C = 200 × 81/100 = 162. A beats C by 200 − 162 = 38 m.

A car travels 240 km in 4 hours. Its AVERAGE SPEED in km/h is:

(A) 50
(B) 60
(C) 65
(D) 70
cards.back:
(B) 60

Time, Speed & Distance — Speed = Distance / Time = 240/4 = 60 km/h.
cards.storedExplanation: Speed = Distance / Time = 240/4 = 60 km/h.

(B) 48 km/h

cards.front:
Two trains of lengths 120 m and 80 m run on parallel tracks in OPPOSITE directions at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. The time they take to pass each other completely is:

Time & Work — Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/8 = 4/24 + 3/24 = 7/24 tank/hr. Time = 24/7 ≈ 3.43 hr ≈ 3 hr 25 min. INSIGHT — TIMES NEVER ADD; RATES DO. Common mistake: students sum up times (6+8=14), wrong. Always think 'rate per hour'. SHORTCUT FORMULA for 2 pipes filling: T_combined = (T_a × T_b)/(T_a + T_b) = 6×8/14 = 48/14 = 24/7. EXTENSION: 3 pipes A, B, C fill in T_a, T_b, T_c — combined = 1/(1/T_a + 1/T_b + 1/T_c). If LEAK (drains), subtract its rate.

cards.front:
Pipe A fills in 12 hr; Pipe B empties full tank in 18 hr. With both open, tank fills in:

(A) 36 hr (slower due to leak)
(B) 30 hr (incorrect estimate)
(C) 6 hr (combined wrong)
(D) 9 hr (incorrect estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 36 hr (slower due to leak)

Time & Work — A fills at 1/12 per hr; B empties at 1/18 per hr (negative). Net rate = 1/12 − 1/18 = 3/36 − 2/36 = 1/36 per hr. Time = 36 hr (fills more slowly than A alone). INSIGHT — when filling rate > emptying, tank still fills, but slowly. If filling rate < emptying, tank can't be filled (eventually empty). FORMULA: net rate = sum of inflow rates − sum of outflow rates. PRACTICAL: water tanks with leaks; bathtubs with drain open + tap on; reservoirs with evaporation losses (a kind of leak).

cards.front:
Three pipes A, B, C fill tank in 4, 6, 12 hr. Together they fill in:

(A) 2 hr (combined fast)
(B) 3 hr (close but wrong)
(C) 4 hr (slowest pipe alone)
(D) 22 hr (sum of times)
cards.back:
(A) 2 hr (combined fast)

Time & Work — Combined rate = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12 = 1/2 per hr. Time = 2 hr. SHORTCUT: LCM denominator approach — find LCM of 4, 6, 12 = 12 (capacity = 12 units). A = 12/4 = 3 units/hr; B = 12/6 = 2; C = 12/12 = 1. Total = 6 units/hr. Time = 12/6 = 2 hr. INSIGHT — LCM method is FAST for multi-pipe problems; works well for any 'work-rate' problem (men, machines, pipes). Always assign LCM as 'total work' to keep numbers integer-friendly.

A = 12/4 = 3 units/hr; B = 12/6 = 2; C = 12/12 = 1. Total = 6 units/hr. Time = 12/6 = 2 hr. INSIGHT — LCM method is FAST for multi-pipe problems; works well for any 'work-rate' problem (men, machines, pipes). Always assign LCM as 'total work' to keep numbers integer-friendly.

cards.front:
A tank fills in 10 hr without leak. With leak, takes 12 hr. Leak alone empties full tank in:

(A) 60 hr (calculated leak rate)
(B) 2 hr (just the difference)
(C) 22 hr (incorrect estimate)
(D) 120 hr (incorrect estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 60 hr (calculated leak rate)

Time & Work — Without leak: rate = 1/10 per hr. With leak: rate = 1/12 per hr (slower). Leak rate = 1/10 − 1/12 = 6/60 − 5/60 = 1/60 per hr. Leak alone empties in 1/(1/60) = 60 hr. INSIGHT — common 'tap + leak' problem. FORMULA: leak alone empty time = (T_with_leak × T_without_leak) / (T_with_leak − T_without_leak) = (12 × 10)/(12 − 10) = 60 hr. WORKS when filling-rate > leak-rate (positive net); otherwise tank never fills.

INSIGHT — common 'tap + leak' problem. FORMULA: leak alone empty time = (T_with_leak × T_without_leak) / (T_with_leak − T_without_leak) = (12 × 10)/(12 − 10) = 60 hr. WORKS when filling-rate > leak-rate (positive net); otherwise tank never fills.

cards.front:
Pipe A fills tank in 20 hr. Pipe B fills in 30 hr. After working together for 5 hr, A is closed. B alone takes how long more?

(A) 17.5 hr more for B alone
(B) 10 hr more for B alone
(C) 25 hr more for B alone
(D) 15 hr more for B alone
cards.back:
(A) 17.5 hr more for B alone

Time & Work — Combined rate = 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 = 1/12 per hr. In 5 hr together: 5/12 of tank done. Remaining = 7/12. B alone fills at 1/30 per hr → time = (7/12)/(1/30) = 7×30/12 = 210/12 = 17.5 hr. SHORTCUT: LCM = 60 (capacity 60 units); A=3 units/hr; B=2; together=5. After 5 hr: 25 units. Remaining = 35. B alone: 35/2 = 17.5 hr. INSIGHT — these 2-stage problems: (1) compute work done in stage 1 with multiple workers; (2) remaining work / single worker rate.

B alone fills at 1/30 per hr → time = (7/12)/(1/30) = 7×30/12 = 210/12 = 17.5 hr. SHORTCUT: LCM = 60 (capacity 60 units); A=3 units/hr; B=2; together=5. After 5 hr: 25 units. Remaining = 35. B alone: 35/2 = 17.5 hr. INSIGHT — these 2-stage problems: (1) compute work done in stage 1 with multiple workers; (2) remaining work / single worker rate.

cards.front:
Pipe A fills 60% of tank, then B alone fills the rest. A fills in 6 hr; B fills in 9 hr. Total time:

(A) 7.2 hr total time taken
(B) 6 hr (only A's time)
(C) 15 hr (sum of times)
(D) 9 hr (only B's time)
cards.back:
(A) 7.2 hr total time taken

Time & Work — A fills 60% alone: time = 0.6 × 6 = 3.6 hr (since A takes 6 hr for 100%). B fills remaining 40% alone: time = 0.4 × 9 = 3.6 hr. Total = 3.6 + 3.6 = 7.2 hr. cards.front:
A tank with a leak empties a full tank in 8 hours. An inlet pipe fills water at the rate of 6 litres/minute. When both the inlet and the leak are open together, the tank is emptied in 12 hours. The capacity of the tank (in litres) is:

(A) 5,760
(B) 8,640
(C) 6,480
(D) 7,200
cards.back:
(B) 8,640

Time & Work — Let capacity = V litres. Leak rate = V/8 per hour (emptying). Inlet = 6 L/min = 360 L/hr (filling). Net emptying rate with both open = V/12 per hour. So V/8 − 360 = V/12. Multiply by 24: 3V − 8640 = 2V → V = 8640 litres. Check: leak rate = 1080 L/hr; inlet = 360 L/hr; net empty 720 L/hr → 8640/720 = 12 h ✓.

cards.front:
Two pipes A and B together can fill a tank in 6 hours. Pipe A alone takes 5 hours less than pipe B. How long does pipe B take alone to fill the tank?

(A) 10 hours
(B) 15 hours
(C) 12 hours
(D) 20 hours
cards.back:
(B) 15 hours

Time & Work — Let B take x hours alone; then A takes (x − 5). Rate A + Rate B = 1/6. 1/(x−5) + 1/x = 1/6. Combine: (x + x − 5) / [x(x−5)] = 1/6 → 6(2x − 5) = x² − 5x → 12x − 30 = x² − 5x → x² − 17x + 30 = 0. Using quadratic formula: x = (17 ± √(289 − 120))/2 = (17 ± 13)/2 → x = 15 or x = 2. x = 2 fails (x − 5 negative). So B = 15 h, A = 10 h. Verify: 1/15 + 1/10 = 2/30 + 3/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 ✓.

cards.front:
A tank can be filled by pipe A in 20 hours. Due to a leak at the bottom it now takes 25 hours to fill. How long would the leak alone empty a full tank?

(A) 80 hours
(B) 100 hours
(C) 120 hours
(D) 60 hours
cards.back:
(B) 100 hours

Time & Work — Rate of A = 1/20. Combined rate (A filling + leak emptying) = 1/25. Leak rate = 1/20 − 1/25 = 5/100 − 4/100 = 1/100 per hour (emptying). So the leak alone empties a full tank in 100 hours. Classic formula: if filling time without leak = t₁ and with leak = t₂, leak-alone time = (t₁ × t₂) / (t₂ − t₁) = (20 × 25) / 5 = 100.

cards.front:
Find the COMPOUND INTEREST on ₹10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years (annual compounding):

(A) ₹2100 (using A=P(1+r)^n)
(B) ₹2000 (simple interest only)
(C) ₹2200 (an over-estimate)
(D) ₹2500 (way over-shot now)
cards.back:
(A) ₹2100 (using A=P(1+r)^n)

Simple & Compound Interest — COMPOUND INTEREST formula: A = P × (1 + r/100)ⁿ, where A = amount, P = principal, r = rate per period, n = number of periods. Plug: A = 10000 × (1.10)² = 10000 × 1.21 = ₹12,100. CI = A − P = 12100 − 10000 = ₹2,100. KEY: in COMPOUND interest, INTEREST IS ADDED TO PRINCIPAL each period; subsequent interest computed on NEW (larger) principal. SIMPLE INTEREST equivalent: SI = PRT/100 = 10000 × 10 × 2 / 100 = ₹2,000. CI − SI for 2 years = ₹100 = P(r/100)² = 10000 × 0.01 = 100 ✓. CRITICAL FORMULAS: (1) A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ — annual compounding. (2) A = P(1 + r/200)^(2n) — half-yearly. (3) A = P(1 + r/400)^(4n) — quarterly. (4) A = P × eᵏᵗ — continuous compounding (k = ln(1+r)). DIFFERENCE FORMULAS: CI − SI for 2 years = P(r/100)²; for 3 years = P(r/100)²(3 + r/100). PRACTICE — quick Pythagoras check: at 10%, after 2 years P doubles roughly (1.21 of original); at 10% rule of 72: doubles in 7.2 years. PYQ FREQUENCY: CI is a SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RBI Grade B 1-mark guarantee.

cards.front:
Find compound interest on ₹8000 at 20% per annum for 1 year, compounded HALF-YEARLY:

(A) ₹1680 (using r/2 each period)
(B) ₹1600 (annual simple here)

Simple & Compound Interest — HALF-YEARLY COMPOUNDING: rate per period = annual rate / 2 = 20%/2 = 10%. Periods in 1 year = 2. A = P × (1 + r/200)^(2n) = 8000 × (1.10)² = 8000 × 1.21 = ₹9,680. CI = ₹9680 − ₹8000 = ₹1,680. CONTRAST WITH ANNUAL CI: at 20% annual: A = 8000 × 1.20 = ₹9,600 → CI = ₹1,600. (3) QUARTERLY: A = P(1 + r/4)^(4n). (4) MONTHLY: A = P(1 + r/12)^(12n). (5) CONTINUOUS: A = P × eʳⁿ (limit as compounding frequency → infinity). MORE FREQUENT compounding → MORE INTEREST. EFFECTIVE ANNUAL RATE (EAR): from a nominal r% compounded n times: EAR = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1. e.g., 20% half-yearly: EAR = (1.10)² − 1 = 0.21 = 21%. INDIA banks: most savings accounts compound QUARTERLY. NRI deposits, FDs vary. PYQ FREQUENCY: half-yearly + quarterly compounding in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1-2× per paper.

The DIFFERENCE between CI and SI on ₹6000 for 2 years at 10% p.a. is:

(B) ₹120 (an over-estimate)
(C) ₹100 (a calc rounding)
(D) ₹30 (an under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) ₹60 (using P × (r/100)²)

Simple & Compound Interest — FORMULA: CI − SI for 2 YEARS = P × (r/100)². Plug: 6000 × (0.10)² = 6000 × 0.01 = ₹60. VERIFY: SI = (6000 × 10 × 2)/100 = ₹1,200. CI = 6000 × (1.10)² − 6000 = 7260 − 6000 = ₹1,260. Difference = 1260 − 1200 = ₹60 ✓. KEY DIFFERENCE FORMULAS: (1) CI − SI for 2 YEARS = P × (r/100)². (2) CI − SI for 3 YEARS = P × (r/100)² × (3 + r/100). PROOF for 2 yrs: CI = P[(1 + r/100)² − 1] = P[1 + 2r/100 + (r/100)² − 1] = P × 2r/100 + P × (r/100)². SI = P × 2r/100. So CI − SI = P × (r/100)². EXAM SHORTCUT: for 2 years, just remember CI − SI = (rate%)² × principal / 10,000. e.g., 5% on 8000 for 2 yr: (5/100)² × 8000 = 0.0025 × 8000 = ₹20. PRACTICE: (a) P=₹15000, r=12%, t=2 yr → diff = 15000 × 0.0144 = ₹216. (b) P=₹8000, r=20%, t=2 yr → diff = 8000 × 0.04 = ₹320. PYQ FREQUENCY: CI−SI difference formula in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
A scooter's value DEPRECIATES by 10% each year. If current value is ₹40,000, value after 2 years is:

(A) ₹32,400 (using A=P(1−r)^n)
(B) ₹36,000 (only 1-year drop)
(C) ₹32,000 (linear depreciation calc)
(D) ₹30,000 (over-depreciated value)
cards.back:
(A) ₹32,400 (using A=P(1−r)^n)

Simple & Compound Interest — DEPRECIATION FORMULA: A = P × (1 − r/100)ⁿ. Plug: A = 40,000 × (0.9)² = 40,000 × 0.81 = ₹32,400. KEY: depreciation is 'reverse compound interest' — each year the value REDUCES by r% of CURRENT value (not original). So linear-thinking 40k − 4k − 4k = 32k is WRONG. PROPER: 40k × 0.9 = 36k after Year 1; 36k × 0.9 = 32.4k after Year 2. PRACTICE: a car worth ₹500,000 depreciating 15% yearly: after 3 years = 500,000 × (0.85)³ = 500,000 × 0.614 = ₹307,063. APPLICATIONS: (1) ASSET DEPRECIATION (cars, machines, electronics). (2) PROPERTY value declines (rare in growing economies). (3) CURRENCY depreciation. (4) REVERSE for INFLATION: prices rise at compound rate; loaf of bread that costs ₹50 today, with 5% annual inflation, costs 50 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ ₹81 in 10 years. CONNECTION TO POPULATION GROWTH: same formula for growth (rising). E.g., a town with 1 lakh population growing 5% yearly: in 10 years = 100,000 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ 162,889. EXAM ANGLE: depreciation problems hidden behind 'value of car/machine/asset after N years'. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
If rate of compound interest is 10% per annum, the principal that gives ₹6620 amount after 2 years is:

(A) ₹5,471.07 (~ 6620/1.21)
(B) ₹6,000 (a simple guess)
(C) ₹5,000 (under-estimate)
(D) ₹5,500 (an under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) ₹5,471.07 (~ 6620/1.21)

Simple & Compound Interest — Apply A = P × (1 + r/100)ⁿ → P = A / (1 + r/100)ⁿ. Plug: P = 6620 / (1.10)² = 6620 / 1.21 ≈ ₹5,471.07. KEY METHOD: 'find principal' = work backward from amount; divide by (1+r)ⁿ. NUMERICAL CHECK: 5471.07 × 1.21 ≈ 6620 ✓. PRACTICE: (1) A = ₹14641, r=10%, n=4 → P = 14641 / 1.4641 = ₹10,000. (2) A = ₹13310, r=10%, n=3 → P = 13310 / 1.331 = ₹10,000. ALL CALCULATIONS use 'reverse-compounding' = 'present value' calculation. INDIA BANKING: PRESENT VALUE concept used in (a) Loan EMI calculation. (b) Discounted cash flow analysis (DCF). (c) Bond pricing. (d) Insurance actuarial work. (e) NPV/IRR for projects. KEY FINANCIAL FORMULAS: (1) FV = PV × (1+r)^n. (2) PV = FV / (1+r)^n. (3) Annuity FV = PMT × [(1+r)^n − 1]/r. (4) Annuity PV = PMT × [1 − (1+r)^−n]/r. PYQ FREQUENCY: CI present-value problems in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B Mains, banking finance MBAs 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Using the RULE OF 72, money DOUBLES at 8% compound interest in approximately:

(A) 9 years (72 ÷ 8 = 9)
(B) 8 years (the rate value used)
(C) 12 years (over-estimate)
(D) 6 years (an under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 9 years (72 ÷ 8 = 9)

Simple & Compound Interest — RULE OF 72: TIME TO DOUBLE ≈ 72 / RATE%. Plug r=8%: 72/8 = 9 years. APPROXIMATION based on calculus: ln(2) ≈ 0.693, so doubling time = 0.693/r ≈ 0.72/r when expressed in % rate. EXACT: at 8% CI, doubling time = log(2)/log(1.08) = 9.006 years. The Rule of 72 is accurate within ~5% for rates of 1-10%. PRACTICE: 'how long does ₹1 lakh take to double at X%?' (1) X=12% → 72/12 = 6 years. (2) X=6% → 72/6 = 12 years. (3) X=4% → 72/4 = 18 years. (4) X=10% → 72/10 = 7.2 years. RELATED: RULE OF 114 for tripling; RULE OF 144 for quadrupling. RULE OF 72 USES: (1) QUICK MENTAL MATH on investment returns. (2) Inflation impact: if inflation = 5%, money's purchasing power halves in 14.4 years. (3) POPULATION DOUBLING: at 1.5% annual growth (typical for India), population doubles in 48 years. (4) RULE OF 70 (less common variant; closer to ln(2)/0.01). HISTORICAL: Rule of 72 known since 1494 (Luca Pacioli, Italian mathematician). EXAM-FAVORITE in finance MCQs: SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI Grade B, GMAT, financial-aptitude rounds. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1× per cycle.

A sum DOUBLES in 5 years at simple interest. In how many years will it QUADRUPLE at the same rate?

(A) 10 years
(B) 15 years
(C) 20 years
(D) 25 years
cards.back:
(B) 15 years

Simple & Compound Interest — If P doubles in 5y → SI = P in 5y → rate = 20% p.a. To quadruple: new SI = 3P → time = 3P/(0.2P) = 15 years.

cards.front:
A sum of ₹5,000 earns simple interest of ₹1,500 in 3 years. The rate of interest per annum is:

(A) 8%
(B) 10%
(C) 12%
(D) 15%

A sum triples itself at simple interest in 16 years. The rate of interest per annum is:

(A) 10%
(B) 12.5%
(C) 15%
(D) 20%
cards.back:
(B) 12.5%

Simple & Compound Interest — If the amount triples, the interest earned is 2 × P (since A = P + SI, and A = 3P). So SI = 2P. Using SI = P × R × T / 100: 2P = P × R × 16 / 100 → 200 = 16R → R = 12.5 %. Shortcut — money multiplies 'n' times when (n−1) × 100 / R = T years.

What principal would amount to ₹7,200 in 4 years at 5% simple interest per annum?

(A) ₹6,000
(B) ₹5,760
(C) ₹7,000
(D) ₹6,500

In how many years will a sum of money double at 8% per annum simple interest?

(A) 10 years
(B) 12.5 years
(C) 15 years
(D) 8 years
cards.back:
(B) 12.5 years

Simple & Compound Interest — Doubling means SI = P. Using SI = P × R × T / 100: P = P × 8 × T / 100 → T = 100 / 8 = 12.5 years. Shortcut for 'n-fold' — Time = 100 × (n−1) / R. Here n=2, R=8 → T = 100 × 1 / 8 = 12.5 years. Do not confuse with compound-interest rule of 72.

cards.front:
A sum of ₹800 at simple interest becomes ₹920 in 3 years. If the rate is increased by 3% p.a., the new amount after 3 years will be:

(A) ₹960
(B) ₹992
(C) ₹975
(D) ₹1,000
cards.back:
(B) ₹992

Simple & Compound Interest — Original SI = 920 − 800 = ₹120 in 3 years. Original rate R = (120 × 100) / (800 × 3) = 5 %. New rate = 5 + 3 = 8 %. New SI = (800 × 8 × 3) / 100 = ₹192. New amount = 800 + 192 = ₹992.

(B) 5%
(C) 6%

cards.back:
(B) 5%

Simple & Compound Interest — Given SI = P/4 in 5 years. Using SI = P × R × T / 100: P/4 = P × R × 5 / 100 → 1/4 = 5R/100 → R = 100 / (4 × 5) = 5 %. Quick sanity-check — at 5 % over 5 years, SI = 25 % of P = P/4. ✓

Mensuration & Geometry — STANDARD VALUES: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2. So sin 30° + cos 60° = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. KEY VALUES TABLE (memorize for SSC, NEET, JEE): sin: 0°=0, 30°=1/2, 45°=1/√2, 60°=√3/2, 90°=1. cos: 0°=1, 30°=√3/2, 45°=1/√2, 60°=1/2, 90°=0. tan: 0°=0, 30°=1/√3, 45°=1, 60°=√3, 90°=∞. COMPLEMENTARY-ANGLE FORMULAS: sin(90°−θ) = cos θ; cos(90°−θ) = sin θ; tan(90°−θ) = cot θ. So sin 30° = cos 60° (since 30° + 60° = 90°). MEMORIZATION TRICK: sin values from 0° to 90° = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2 = 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1. cos values are the reverse. PYTHAGOREAN IDENTITY: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (always). PYQ FREQUENCY: standard angle values are a top SSC, JEE-Main, NEET 1-mark guarantee.

MEMORIZATION TRICK: sin values from 0° to 90° = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2 = 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1. cos values are the reverse. PYTHAGOREAN IDENTITY: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (always). PYQ FREQUENCY: standard angle values are a top SSC, JEE-Main, NEET 1-mark guarantee.

cards.front:
If sin θ = 3/5, then cos θ equals (assuming θ in first quadrant):

(A) 4/5 (using Pythagoras)
(B) 5/3 (the reciprocal value)
(C) 5/4 (some other ratio here)
(D) 3/4 (a different fraction)
cards.back:
(A) 4/5 (using Pythagoras)

Mensuration & Geometry — Use the IDENTITY sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. So cos²θ = 1 − (3/5)² = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25. Therefore cos θ = ±4/5. In first quadrant (0° to 90°), cos θ > 0, so cos θ = 4/5. INTERPRETATION: in a right triangle, if sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = 3/5, then opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5; by Pythagoras adjacent = √(25−9) = √16 = 4. So cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse = 4/5. THE 3-4-5 TRIANGLE is the most famous Pythagorean triple — students should recognize it instantly. OTHER COMMON TRIPLES: (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25). KEY METHOD: when given one trig ratio, draw a right triangle, label the two known sides, find the third via Pythagoras, then read off any other ratio. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'find cos given sin' or vice-versa is a 1-mark guarantee in SSC CGL, JEE-Main. Quadrant sign awareness becomes critical in Class 11+ trig.

cards.front:
The value of tan 45° + cot 45° equals:

(A) 2 (sum of two ones)
(B) 1 (a single unit value)
(C) 0 (cancellation result)
(D) √2 (an irrational value)
cards.back:
(A) 2 (sum of two ones)

Mensuration & Geometry — tan 45° = 1, cot 45° = 1 (since cot = 1/tan). So tan 45° + cot 45° = 1 + 1 = 2. WHY tan 45° = 1? At 45°, sin = cos = 1/√2; so tan = sin/cos = 1. Same for cot. UNIQUE PROPERTY: 45° is the ONLY acute angle where tan θ = cot θ = 1 — useful for IDENTIFYING the angle in problems like 'tan A = cot A → A = 45°'. RECIPROCAL PAIRS: sin/csc, cos/sec, tan/cot. PRODUCTS: sin × csc = 1, cos × sec = 1, tan × cot = 1 (for any θ where defined). SAMPLE TRAP: 'tan 30° + cot 60°' — many students think they're equal (both = 1/√3); actually they ARE equal (cot 60° = 1/tan 60° = 1/√3 = tan 30°). PYQ ANGLE: standard-angle arithmetic appears 2-3× per JEE-Main, SSC CGL, NEET-style trig. KEY METHOD: memorize the value table, apply identities.

cards.front:
If tan θ = 1, then sin²θ + cos²θ + tan²θ equals:

(A) 2 (Pythagoras gives one + one)
(B) 1 (only the basic identity)
(C) 3 (a larger sum value)
(D) 1/2 (a fraction result)
cards.back:
(A) 2 (Pythagoras gives one + one)

Mensuration & Geometry — PYTHAGOREAN IDENTITY: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 — ALWAYS holds for any θ. tan θ = 1 → tan²θ = 1. So sin²θ + cos²θ + tan²θ = 1 + 1 = 2. ANGLE: tan θ = 1 → θ = 45° (in first quadrant). CHECK: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2; sin² + cos² = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 ✓. tan² = 1 ✓. Sum = 2 ✓. KEY IDENTITIES (memorize for SSC/JEE/NEET): (1) sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. (2) 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. (3) 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ. APPLICATION — examiners build composite expressions to test which identity applies. SHORTCUT: anytime you see sin² + cos² in an expression, INSTANTLY replace with 1. PYQ FREQUENCY: identity-application Qs are 1-2 per JEE-Main, NEET, SSC CGL Tier 2 paper. EXAM TIP: don't compute sin/cos individually — apply identity first to simplify.

cards.front:
What is the value of sec²60° − tan²60°?

(A) 1 (per Pythagorean identity)
(B) 0 (the difference is zero)
(C) 3 (a positive integer value)
(D) −1 (a negative integer value)
cards.back:
(A) 1 (per Pythagorean identity)

Mensuration & Geometry — PYTHAGOREAN IDENTITY: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ → sec²θ − tan²θ = 1. This holds for ANY θ where sec θ is defined (θ ≠ 90°, 270°, etc.). So sec²60° − tan²60° = 1. VERIFY: sec 60° = 1/cos 60° = 1/(1/2) = 2 → sec²60° = 4. tan 60° = √3 → tan²60° = 3. Difference: 4 − 3 = 1 ✓. INSIGHT: examiners love this 'derive-and-verify' style — the IDENTITY gives the answer immediately, but plugging numbers also works (slower). PARALLEL IDENTITY: csc²θ − cot²θ = 1 (for θ ≠ 0°, 180°). MEMORIZATION TIP: there are 3 Pythagorean identities — one for each pair (sin/cos, sec/tan, csc/cot). Each comes from sin² + cos² = 1 by dividing by sin² or cos². PYQ FREQUENCY: identity-direct Qs are 1-2× per JEE-Main, SSC. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests fast-recall of the three identities; bonus for shortcut.

cards.front:
A pole of height 10 m casts a shadow of length 10√3 m. The angle of elevation of the sun is:

(A) 30° (above the horizontal)
(B) 45° (a half right angle)
(C) 60° (a steeper elevation)
(D) 90° (sun directly overhead)
cards.back:
(A) 30° (above the horizontal)

Mensuration & Geometry — tan(angle of elevation) = OPPOSITE / ADJACENT = pole-height / shadow-length = 10 / (10√3) = 1/√3. tan 30° = 1/√3, so angle = 30°. INTERPRETATION: when the sun is LOWER in the sky, shadows are LONGER — and the angle of elevation is SMALLER. SUN OVERHEAD (noon at equator): angle = 90°, shadow = 0 (theoretically). DAWN/DUSK: angle approaches 0°, shadow approaches infinity. PRACTICAL EXAMPLE: this is exactly how the great Egyptian astronomer ERATOSTHENES (~240 BCE) computed Earth's circumference — by comparing shadow lengths at Alexandria and Syene at solar noon. KEY METHOD for height-distance: (1) draw a right triangle. (2) identify opposite/adjacent. (3) use tan = opposite/adjacent. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 height-distance Qs per SSC CGL Tier 2; JEE-Main rarely. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests trig-ratio recognition + practical-geometry application.

cards.front:
Simplify: sin 60° · cos 30° + cos 60° · sin 30°.

(A) 1 (equals sin 90°)
(B) 0 (cancellation occurs)
(C) 1/2 (a half-value result)
(D) √3/2 (with root three)
cards.back:
(A) 1 (equals sin 90°)

Mensuration & Geometry — Apply ANGLE-SUM IDENTITY: sin(A + B) = sin A · cos B + cos A · sin B. So sin 60° · cos 30° + cos 60° · sin 30° = sin(60° + 30°) = sin 90° = 1. DIRECT VERIFY: (√3/2)(√3/2) + (1/2)(1/2) = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1 ✓. ANGLE-SUM/DIFFERENCE IDENTITIES (memorize): (1) sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B. (2) sin(A−B) = sin A cos B − cos A sin B. (3) cos(A+B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B. (4) cos(A−B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B. KEY FOR JEE-MAIN: lots of trig simplification problems hide angle-sum patterns — students who recognize the pattern solve in seconds. EXAM TRAP: many students compute each term separately (slow); spotting the identity is the elite shortcut. INSIGHT: this also gives derivation of double-angle: sin 2A = sin(A+A) = 2 sin A cos A. PYQ FREQUENCY: trigonometric simplification = 2-3 Qs per JEE-Main, NEET physics-side.

cards.front:
If 3x + 7 = 25, then x equals:

(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 7
(D) 8
cards.back:
(B) 6

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 3x + 7 = 25 → 3x = 18 → x = 6. Distractor 5 corresponds to the error of subtracting 7/3 (≈2.3) instead of 7. Distractor 7 comes from solving 3x = 21 (forgetting the 25 on the right). Distractor 8 from solving 3x = 24.

cards.front:
If x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, what is the value of x?

(A) 5
(B) 7
(C) 6
(D) 8
cards.back:
(B) 7

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Add the two equations: 2x = 14 → x = 7. Then y = 3. Distractor 5 from averaging without solving (10/2). Distractor 6 from x = (10−4) wrongly. Distractor 8 from sub-error 10−2 = 8.

cards.front:
The roots of the quadratic x² − 5x + 6 = 0 are:

(A) 1 and 6
(B) 2 and 3
(C) −2 and −3
(D) −1 and −6
cards.back:
(B) 2 and 3

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Factor: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). Roots = 2, 3. Sum = 5, product = 6 (Vieta's). Distractor 1,6 — sum 7, product 6: matches product but not sum. Distractor −2,−3 — sum −5 (wrong sign). −1,−6 — sum −7, product 6: wrong sign on sum.

cards.front:
If a + b = 7 and ab = 12, the value of a² + b² is:

(A) 49
(B) 25
(C) 37
(D) 73
cards.back:
(B) 25

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Use identity (a+b)² = a² + b² + 2ab. So a²+b² = (a+b)² − 2ab = 49 − 24 = 25. Distractor 49 = the squared sum, no subtraction. Distractor 37 = 49 − 12 (subtracted ab once instead of 2ab). Distractor 73 = 49 + 24 (added instead of subtracted).

cards.front:
The sum of the roots of the quadratic 2x² − 6x + 4 = 0 is:

(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) −3
(D) 6
cards.back:
(B) 3

Algebra, Probability & Stats — For ax² + bx + c = 0, sum of roots = −b/a = −(−6)/2 = 3. Verify by factoring: 2x² − 6x + 4 = 2(x² − 3x + 2) = 2(x−1)(x−2); roots 1 and 2; sum = 3. Distractor 2 = product of roots (c/a = 4/2). Distractor −3 = sign error (−b read as b). Distractor 6 = took −b without dividing by a.

Distractor 2 = product of roots (c/a = 4/2). Distractor −3 = sign error (−b read as b). Distractor 6 = took −b without dividing by a.

cards.front:
If x² − y² = 27 and x + y = 9, then x − y equals:

(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 4
(D) 9
cards.back:
(B) 3

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Identity: x² − y² = (x+y)(x−y) → 27 = 9(x−y) → x−y = 3. Then from x+y = 9 and x−y = 3, x = 6, y = 3. Distractor 2 from misreading 27/(9+1). Distractor 4 from 36/9 (squaring error). Distractor 9 from copying x+y without using identity.

cards.front:
If 2x − 3y = 7 and 4x + 5y = 25, the value of y is:

(A) 2
(B) 1
(C) 3
(D) −1
cards.back:
(B) 1

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Multiply first equation by 2: 4x − 6y = 14. Subtract from second: (4x+5y) − (4x−6y) = 25 − 14 → 11y = 11 → y = 1. Then 2x = 7 + 3(1) = 10, x = 5. Verify: 4(5)+5(1) = 25 ✓. Distractor 2 from mis-aligning coefficients. Distractor 3 from solving for x not y. Distractor −1 from sign-flip during elimination.

Distractor 2 from mis-aligning coefficients. Distractor 3 from solving for x not y. Distractor −1 from sign-flip during elimination.

cards.front:
If A > B, B = C, C ≥ D, then which is definitely true?

(A) A > D, by chain of inequalities
(B) A < D, the reverse direction here
(C) A = D, equality from chain steps
(D) B < D, only sometimes true
cards.back:
(A) A > D, by chain of inequalities

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Combine: A > B, B = C, so A > C. C ≥ D, so A > C ≥ D → A > D (definitely true). Distractor 2 is opposite. Distractor 3 only equality if D = C and B = A, but A > B, not =, so equality is impossible. Distractor 4 — B = C ≥ D, so B ≥ D (could be B = D, never B < D).
cards.option1: A < D, the reverse direction here
cards.option2: A = D, equality from chain steps

cards.front:
If P ≥ Q, Q > R, R = S, S ≤ T, which is NOT necessarily true?

(A) P > R, definitely from given chain
(B) P > T, NOT definitely from chain
(C) Q > S, definitely from chain
(D) P > S, definitely from chain
cards.back:
(B) P > T, NOT definitely from chain

Algebra, Probability & Stats — P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T. So P ≥ Q > R = S, hence P > R, P > S, Q > S — all definite. But for P vs T: we have P ≥ S (since P > S follows). And S ≤ T means T could be larger or equal to S. So T could be > P (if T is much larger) or T ≤ P. Hence P > T is NOT guaranteed. ✓
cards.option1: P > R, definitely from given chain

cards.front:
If x is an integer and 2x + 5 < 17, the LARGEST possible value of x is:

(A) 5 is the largest integer here
(B) 6 is the largest integer here
(C) 7 is the largest integer here
(D) 4 is the largest integer here
cards.back:
(A) 5 is the largest integer here

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 2x + 5 < 17 → 2x < 12 → x < 6. Largest INTEGER < 6 is 5. Verify: 2(5)+5 = 15 < 17 ✓. 2(6)+5 = 17 NOT < 17. Distractor 6 = boundary exclusion error. Distractor 7 = wrong direction. Distractor 4 = answered ≤ 5 wrongly.
cards.storedExplanation: 2x + 5 < 17 → 2x < 12 → x < 6. Largest INTEGER < 6 is 5. Verify: 2(5)+5 = 15 < 17 ✓. 2(6)+5 = 17 NOT < 17. Distractor 6 = boundary exclusion error. Distractor 7 = wrong direction. Distractor 4 = answered ≤ 5 wrongly.

cards.front:
Solve for y: 3y − 7 ≥ 2y + 5

(A) y ≥ 12 satisfies the inequality
(B) y ≥ 5 satisfies the inequality
(C) y ≤ 12 satisfies the inequality
(D) y ≤ 5 satisfies the inequality
cards.back:
(A) y ≥ 12 satisfies the inequality

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 3y − 7 ≥ 2y + 5 → 3y − 2y ≥ 5 + 7 → y ≥ 12. Verify y = 12: 3(12)−7 = 29; 2(12)+5 = 29. 29 ≥ 29 ✓. y = 13: 32 ≥ 31 ✓. Distractor 2 — used 7 + 2 wrongly. Distractor 3 — wrong sign direction. Distractor 4 — wrong both.
cards.storedExplanation: 3y − 7 ≥ 2y + 5 → 3y − 2y ≥ 5 + 7 → y ≥ 12. Verify y = 12: 3(12)−7 = 29; 2(12)+5 = 29. 29 ≥ 29 ✓. y = 13: 32 ≥ 31 ✓. Distractor 2 — used 7 + 2 wrongly. Distractor 3 — wrong sign direction. Distractor 4 — wrong both.

cards.front:
Solve: −2x ≥ 8 (note negative coefficient).

(A) x ≥ −4, with the sign retained
(B) x ≤ −4, sign FLIPS on negative divide
(C) x ≥ 4, with the positive answer
(D) x ≤ 4, the positive answer here
cards.back:
(B) x ≤ −4, sign FLIPS on negative divide

Algebra, Probability & Stats — −2x ≥ 8 → divide both sides by −2. CRUCIAL RULE: when multiplying/dividing both sides of an inequality by a NEGATIVE number, FLIP the inequality sign. So x ≤ 8/(−2) = −4. Verify x = −5: −2(−5) = 10 ≥ 8 ✓. x = −4: −2(−4) = 8 ≥ 8 ✓. x = 0: 0 ≥ 8 ✗.
cards.storedExplanation: −2x ≥ 8 → divide both sides by −2. CRUCIAL RULE: when multiplying/dividing both sides of an inequality by a NEGATIVE number, FLIP the inequality sign. So x ≤ 8/(−2) = −4. Verify x = −5: −2(−5) = 10 ≥ 8 ✓. x = −4: −2(−4) = 8 ≥ 8 ✓. x = 0: 0 ≥ 8 ✗.

cards.front:
If 5 < x < 12 and x is an integer, the SUM of all possible values of x is:

(A) 63 from arithmetic-miscount answer
(B) 51 from sum of 6 to 11 inclusive
(C) 75 from arithmetic-miscount answer
(D) 68 if endpoints 5 and 12 included
cards.back:
(B) 51 from sum of 6 to 11 inclusive

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Strict inequalities: 5 < x < 12 → x ∈ {6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11}. Sum = 6+7+8+9+10+11 = 6×(6+11)/2 = 6×17/2 = 51. Distractor 68 = if you wrongly include 5 + 12: that gives 5+6+...+12 = 8×17/2 = 68. Distractor 63 = arithmetic slip. Distractor 75 = miscount.
cards.storedExplanation: Strict inequalities: 5 < x < 12 → x ∈ {6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11}. Sum = 6+7+8+9+10+11 = 6×(6+11)/2 = 6×17/2 = 51. Distractor 68 = if you wrongly include 5 + 12: that gives 5+6+...+12 = 8×17/2 = 68. Distractor 63 = arithmetic slip. Distractor 75 = miscount.

cards.front:
If a < b < c and all are positive, then which is largest in 1/a, 1/b, 1/c?

(A) 1/a is the largest reciprocal
(B) 1/c is the largest reciprocal
(C) 1/b is the largest reciprocal
(D) All reciprocals are equal
cards.back:
(A) 1/a is the largest reciprocal

Algebra, Probability & Stats — For positive numbers, smallest denominator → largest fraction. a < b < c (a smallest), so 1/a > 1/b > 1/c. Reciprocal REVERSES order for positive numbers. Example: a=2, b=3, c=4 → 1/a = 0.5, 1/b = 0.33, 1/c = 0.25. So 1/a largest.
cards.storedExplanation: For positive numbers, smallest denominator → largest fraction. a < b < c (a smallest), so 1/a > 1/b > 1/c. Reciprocal REVERSES order for positive numbers. Example: a=2, b=3, c=4 → 1/a = 0.5, 1/b = 0.33, 1/c = 0.25. So 1/a largest.

cards.front:
In how many ways can the letters of the word 'WORLD' be arranged?

(A) 60
(B) 120
(C) 720
(D) 24
cards.back:
(B) 120

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 5 distinct letters → 5! = 120. Basic permutation without repetition.
cards.storedExplanation: 5 distinct letters → 5! = 120. Basic permutation without repetition.

cards.front:
Number of arrangements of the letters of 'LEVEL':

(A) 120
(B) 30
(C) 60
(D) 15
cards.back:
(B) 30

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 5 letters with repetitions L(2), E(2), V(1). Arrangements = 5!/(2!·2!) = 120/4 = 30.
cards.storedExplanation: 5 letters with repetitions L(2), E(2), V(1). Arrangements = 5!/(2!·2!) = 120/4 = 30.

cards.front:
How many 3-letter arrangements can be formed from 8 distinct letters (no repetition)?

(A) 56
(B) 336
(C) 120
(D) 512
cards.back:
(B) 336

Algebra, Probability & Stats — nPr = n!/(n−r)! = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. Distractor 56 is 8C3 (combinations); 512 is 8³ (with repetition).
cards.storedExplanation: nPr = n!/(n−r)! = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. Distractor 56 is 8C3 (combinations); 512 is 8³ (with repetition).

cards.front:
In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table?

(A) 120
(B) 24
(C) 60
(D) 20
cards.back:
(B) 24

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Circular arrangements of n distinct persons = (n−1)! = 4! = 24. The subtraction accounts for rotational equivalence — only relative positions matter.
cards.storedExplanation: Circular arrangements of n distinct persons = (n−1)! = 4! = 24. The subtraction accounts for rotational equivalence — only relative positions matter.

cards.front:
A committee of 3 is to be formed from 5 men and 4 women with at least 1 woman. Total ways:

(A) 74
(B) 84
(C) 60
(D) 90
cards.back:
(A) 74

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total committees without restriction = 9C3 = 84. Committees with NO woman (all men) = 5C3 = 10. At-least-1-woman = 84 − 10 = 74. Complement trick is cleaner than summing cases.
cards.storedExplanation: Total committees without restriction = 9C3 = 84. Committees with NO woman (all men) = 5C3 = 10. At-least-1-woman = 84 − 10 = 74. Complement trick is cleaner than summing cases.

cards.front:
Number of ways to choose 2 cards from a standard 52-card deck:

(A) 1326
(B) 2652
(C) 52
(D) 104
cards.back:
(A) 1326

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Order doesn't matter → combination. 52C2 = 52·51/2 = 1326. Distractor 2652 = 52P2 counts order.
cards.storedExplanation: Order doesn't matter → combination. 52C2 = 52·51/2 = 1326. Distractor 2652 = 52P2 counts order.

cards.front:
How many arrangements of the letters of 'MISSISSIPPI' are there?

(A) 34650
(B) 39916800
(C) 831600
(D) 990
cards.back:
(A) 34650

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 11 letters with repetitions M(1), I(4), S(4), P(2). Arrangements = 11!/(4!·4!·2!·1!) = 39,916,800 / (24·24·2) = 39,916,800 / 1152 = 34,650.

cards.front:
In how many ways can 4 boys and 3 girls sit in a row so that all girls sit together?

(A) 720
(B) 5040
(C) 120
(D) 144
cards.back:
(A) 720

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Treat the 3 girls as ONE unit → 4 boys + 1 girl-block = 5 units → 5! = 120. Within the girl-block, 3 girls can permute in 3! = 6 ways. Total = 120 × 6 = 720. Classic 'bundle together' technique.

cards.front:
The number of ways the letters of the word 'ROAD' can be arranged is:

(A) 12
(B) 24
(C) 16
(D) 36
cards.back:
(B) 24

Algebra, Probability & Stats — All four letters of ROAD are distinct, so number of arrangements = 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. Whenever letters are distinct, total = n!. If a letter were repeated, divide by the factorial of the repetition count — e.g. 'BOOK' has 2 O's so total = 4! / 2! = 12.

cards.front:
From a group of 8 men, in how many ways can a committee of 3 be selected?

(A) 24
(B) 56
(C) 336
(D) 112

cards.front:
In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table?

(A) 120
(B) 24
(C) 60
(D) 12

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Circular arrangements — fix one person to break rotational symmetry; the rest can be arranged in (n − 1)! ways. So 5 people → 4! = 24. SSC convention: by default, reflections distinct → answer 24.

cards.front:
How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1 to 9 if no digit is repeated?

(A) 6,561
(B) 3,024
(C) 9,000
(D) 362,880
cards.back:
(B) 3,024

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 9 distinct digits, choose and arrange 4 of them in order — ⁹P₄ = 9! / 5! = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3,024. Trap 6,561 = 9⁴ (with repetition allowed). Trap 9,000 = total 4-digit numbers using 0-9 (1000 to 9999). Trap 362,880 = 9!.
cards.storedExplanation: 9 distinct digits, choose and arrange 4 of them in order — ⁹P₄ = 9! / 5! = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3,024. Trap 6,561 = 9⁴ (with repetition allowed). Trap 9,000 = total 4-digit numbers using 0-9 (1000 to 9999). Trap 362,880 = 9!.

(A) 180
(B) 195
(C) 210
(D) 120
cards.back:
(B) 195

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total ways without restriction = ¹⁰C₄ = 210. Ways with NO girl (all boys) = ⁶C₄ = 15. So at-least-1-girl = 210 − 15 = 195. The 'complement' trick — easier than summing 1G+3B + 2G+2B + 3G+1B + 4G+0B = 60 + 90 + 40 + 1 = 191. Hmm — let me re-verify. ⁴C₁·⁶C₃ + ⁴C₂·⁶C₂ + ⁴C₃·⁶C₁ + ⁴C₄·⁶C₀ = 4·20 + 6·15 + 4·6 + 1·1 = 80 + 90 + 24 + 1 = 195 ✓. Both methods agree.

The 'complement' trick — easier than summing 1G+3B + 2G+2B + 3G+1B + 4G+0B = 60 + 90 + 40 + 1 = 191. Hmm — let me re-verify. ⁴C₁·⁶C₃ + ⁴C₂·⁶C₂ + ⁴C₃·⁶C₁ + ⁴C₄·⁶C₀ = 4·20 + 6·15 + 4·6 + 1·1 = 80 + 90 + 24 + 1 = 195 ✓. Both methods agree.

cards.front:
The number of ways the letters of the word 'NUMBER' can be arranged so that the vowels U and E always remain together is:

(A) 120
(B) 240
(C) 360
(D) 720
cards.back:
(B) 240

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Standard 'group-the-bound-pair' technique. Treat (UE) or (EU) as a single block — now we have 5 distinct items to arrange: N, M, B, R, (vowel-pair). 5! = 120 arrangements. The vowel-pair internally can be UE or EU = 2 ways. Total = 120 × 2 = 240. Always: arrange the n−k+1 'items' first, then multiply by k! for internal arrangements of the bound block.
cards.storedExplanation: Standard 'group-the-bound-pair' technique. Treat (UE) or (EU) as a single block — now we have 5 distinct items to arrange: N, M, B, R, (vowel-pair). 5! = 120 arrangements. The vowel-pair internally can be UE or EU = 2 ways. Total = 120 × 2 = 240. Always: arrange the n−k+1 'items' first, then multiply by k! for internal arrangements of the bound block.

cards.front:
A fair coin is tossed once. The probability of getting a head is:

(A) 1/4
(B) 1/2
(C) 1/3
(D) 1
cards.back:
(B) 1/2

Algebra, Probability & Stats — P(head) = favourable / total = 1/2. Basic template for every probability problem.
cards.storedExplanation: P(head) = favourable / total = 1/2. Basic template for every probability problem.

A fair die is rolled. The probability of getting an even number is:

(A) 1/6
(B) 1/2
(C) 1/3
(D) 2/3
cards.back:
(B) 1/2

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Even outcomes = {2, 4, 6} → 3 favourable out of 6. P = 3/6 = 1/2. Same as P(odd).
cards.storedExplanation: Even outcomes = {2, 4, 6} → 3 favourable out of 6. P = 3/6 = 1/2. Same as P(odd).

cards.front:
Two fair dice are rolled. The probability of getting a sum of 7 is:

(A) 1/12
(B) 1/6
(C) 1/4
(D) 1/9
cards.back:
(B) 1/6

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total outcomes = 36. Sum-7 pairs: (1,6)(6,1)(2,5)(5,2)(3,4)(4,3) = 6. P = 6/36 = 1/6. Sum-7 is the MOST LIKELY sum — peak of the dice-sum distribution.

From a standard deck of 52 cards, one card is drawn. The probability it is a King is:

(A) 1/52
(B) 1/13
(C) 1/4
(D) 4/52 simplified different
cards.back:
(B) 1/13

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 4 Kings in 52 cards. P = 4/52 = 1/13. Cache the deck: 52 = 4 suits × 13 ranks. 12 face cards (J, Q, K of each suit).
cards.storedExplanation: 4 Kings in 52 cards. P = 4/52 = 1/13. Cache the deck: 52 = 4 suits × 13 ranks. 12 face cards (J, Q, K of each suit).

cards.front:
A bag has 5 red and 7 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. P(red) is:

(A) 5/7
(B) 5/12
(C) 7/12
(D) 1/5
cards.back:
(B) 5/12

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total = 12, favourable (red) = 5 → P = 5/12. P(blue) = 7/12. P(red) + P(blue) = 1 — sanity check.
cards.storedExplanation: Total = 12, favourable (red) = 5 → P = 5/12. P(blue) = 7/12. P(red) + P(blue) = 1 — sanity check.

cards.front:
From a deck of 52 cards, a card is drawn. P(it is a red card or a King) =

(A) 28/52
(B) 26/52
(C) 30/52
(D) 32/52
cards.back:
(A) 28/52

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Addition rule with overlap: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). Reds = 26, Kings = 4, Red Kings = 2 (hearts K, diamonds K). Total = 26 + 4 − 2 = 28. P = 28/52.
cards.storedExplanation: Addition rule with overlap: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). Reds = 26, Kings = 4, Red Kings = 2 (hearts K, diamonds K). Total = 26 + 4 − 2 = 28. P = 28/52.

cards.front:
Two coins are tossed. P(at least one head) =

(A) 1/4
(B) 3/4
(C) 1/2
(D) 1/3
cards.back:
(B) 3/4

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Use complement. P(no head) = P(TT) = 1/4. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Verify by enumeration: HH, HT, TH, TT — 3 of 4 have ≥ 1 head.
cards.storedExplanation: Use complement. P(no head) = P(TT) = 1/4. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Verify by enumeration: HH, HT, TH, TT — 3 of 4 have ≥ 1 head.

cards.front:
Two dice are rolled. P(doublet, i.e. both dice show same number) =

(A) 1/6
(B) 1/12
(C) 1/3
(D) 1/9
cards.back:
(A) 1/6

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Doublets = (1,1), (2,2), …, (6,6) → 6 outcomes out of 36. P = 6/36 = 1/6.

cards.front:
A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. The probability that a randomly drawn ball is BLUE is:

(A) 5/8 (the red fraction)
(B) 3/8 (the blue fraction)
(C) 1/2 (assumes equal split)
(D) 3/5 (blue divided by red)
cards.back:
(B) 3/8 (the blue fraction)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — P(blue) = blue / total = 3 / (5+3) = 3/8. Distractor 1 swaps numerator (gives red probability). Distractor 3 ignores the actual counts. Distractor 4 uses the wrong denominator (just red).
cards.storedExplanation: P(blue) = blue / total = 3 / (5+3) = 3/8. Distractor 1 swaps numerator (gives red probability). Distractor 3 ignores the actual counts. Distractor 4 uses the wrong denominator (just red).

cards.front:
Two dice are tossed together. The probability that the SUM is 7 is:

(A) 5/36 (one fewer than the actual count)
(B) 6/36 = 1/6 (six favourable pairs)
(C) 7/36 (taken from the sum value)
(D) 1/12 (half of the correct value)
cards.back:
(B) 6/36 = 1/6 (six favourable pairs)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Pairs giving sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs. P = 6/36 = 1/6. Sum 7 is the most likely outcome with two fair dice. Distractor 1 = 5/36 (sum 6 or 8). Distractor 3 = 7/36 (no valid pairing). Distractor 4 = halves the answer.
cards.storedExplanation: Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Pairs giving sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs. P = 6/36 = 1/6. Sum 7 is the most likely outcome with two fair dice. Distractor 1 = 5/36 (sum 6 or 8). Distractor 3 = 7/36 (no valid pairing). Distractor 4 = halves the answer.

cards.front:
From a pack of 52 cards, the probability of drawing a KING is:

(A) 1/52 (a single specified card)
(B) 1/13 (any one of four kings)
(C) 1/4 (any one of four suits)
(D) 3/13 (any J, Q or K card)
cards.back:
(B) 1/13 (any one of four kings)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 4 kings (one per suit) in 52 cards. P = 4/52 = 1/13. Distractor 1 — single card. Distractor 3 = 13/52 = 1/4 (any suit). Distractor 4 = 12/52 = 3/13 (any face card: J, Q, K).
cards.storedExplanation: 4 kings (one per suit) in 52 cards. P = 4/52 = 1/13. Distractor 1 — single card. Distractor 3 = 13/52 = 1/4 (any suit). Distractor 4 = 12/52 = 3/13 (any face card: J, Q, K).

cards.front:
If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5 and the events are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, then P(A or B) =

(A) 0.2 (the product of probabilities)
(B) 0.9 (the sum of probabilities)
(C) 0.7 (an arbitrary combined value)
(D) 0.5 (the larger of the two)
cards.back:
(B) 0.9 (the sum of probabilities)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0. So P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.9. Distractor 1 = product (gives joint probability of INDEPENDENT events, not 'or'). Distractor 3 from arbitrary combination. Distractor 4 ignores the additive rule.
cards.storedExplanation: Mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0. So P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.9. Distractor 1 = product (gives joint probability of INDEPENDENT events, not 'or'). Distractor 3 from arbitrary combination. Distractor 4 ignores the additive rule.

cards.front:
A coin is tossed 3 times. The probability of getting EXACTLY 2 heads is:

(A) 1/4 (random guess)
(B) 3/8 (correct binomial value)
(C) 1/2 (half because equal heads/tails)
(D) 1/8 (one specific sequence only)
cards.back:
(B) 3/8 (correct binomial value)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — 3 tosses: 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes. Exactly 2 heads can occur in C(3,2) = 3 ways: HHT, HTH, THH. P = 3/8. Binomial: P = C(3,2) × (1/2)² × (1/2)¹ = 3 × 1/8 = 3/8. Distractor 1 = 1/4 random guess. Distractor 3 = 1/2 confused with at-least-1-head. Distractor 4 = 1/8 (probability of one specific outcome).
cards.storedExplanation: 3 tosses: 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes. Exactly 2 heads can occur in C(3,2) = 3 ways: HHT, HTH, THH. P = 3/8. Binomial: P = C(3,2) × (1/2)² × (1/2)¹ = 3 × 1/8 = 3/8. Distractor 1 = 1/4 random guess. Distractor 3 = 1/2 confused with at-least-1-head. Distractor 4 = 1/8 (probability of one specific outcome).

cards.front:
The probability of an event A NOT occurring equals:

(A) 1 + P(A) (sum greater than 1)
(B) 1 − P(A) (the complement rule)
(C) P(A) ÷ 2 (an arbitrary halving)
(D) P(A) × 0 (yields zero always)
cards.back:
(B) 1 − P(A) (the complement rule)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Complement Rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Total probability is 1; everything not-A is the rest. Useful for 'at least one' problems: P(at least 1) = 1 − P(none). Distractor 1 — sum exceeds 1, impossible for valid probability. Distractor 3 — arbitrary. Distractor 4 — would always give zero.
cards.storedExplanation: Complement Rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Total probability is 1; everything not-A is the rest. Useful for 'at least one' problems: P(at least 1) = 1 − P(none). Distractor 1 — sum exceeds 1, impossible for valid probability. Distractor 3 — arbitrary. Distractor 4 — would always give zero.

cards.front:
Two cards are drawn at random WITHOUT REPLACEMENT from a standard deck of 52. The probability that BOTH are aces is:

(A) 1/169 (independent multiplication)
(B) 1/221 (correct dependent value)
(C) 4/52 (one ace probability)
(D) 1/52 (a single ace fraction)
cards.back:
(B) 1/221 (correct dependent value)

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Without replacement: P(1st ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. P(2nd ace given 1st was ace) = 3/51 = 1/17. P(both) = 1/13 × 1/17 = 1/221. Distractor 1 = (4/52)² = 1/169 (independent multiplication, valid only WITH replacement). Distractor 3 = single-ace probability. Distractor 4 from another wrong reading.
cards.storedExplanation: Without replacement: P(1st ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. P(2nd ace given 1st was ace) = 3/51 = 1/17. P(both) = 1/13 × 1/17 = 1/221. Distractor 1 = (4/52)² = 1/169 (independent multiplication, valid only WITH replacement). Distractor 3 = single-ace probability. Distractor 4 from another wrong reading.

cards.front:
A fair die is rolled once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:

(A) 1/2
(B) 1/3
(C) 1/6
(D) 2/3
cards.back:
(B) 1/3

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6. Favourable outcomes (>4) = {5, 6}, n(E) = 2. Probability = 2/6 = 1/3. Read 'greater than 4' carefully — it does NOT include 4 itself. If it were 'at least 4', the favourable set would be {4, 5, 6} → 3/6 = 1/2.
cards.storedExplanation: Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6. Favourable outcomes (>4) = {5, 6}, n(E) = 2. Probability = 2/6 = 1/3. Read 'greater than 4' carefully — it does NOT include 4 itself. If it were 'at least 4', the favourable set would be {4, 5, 6} → 3/6 = 1/2.

cards.front:
Two fair coins are tossed simultaneously. The probability of getting at least one head is:

(A) 1/4
(B) 3/4
(C) 1/2
(D) 1
cards.back:
(B) 3/4

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, |S| = 4. 'At least one head' = complement of 'no head' (= TT). P(no head) = 1/4. P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Direct count: HH, HT, TH all qualify → 3/4 ✓. The complementary trick (1 − P(none)) is invaluable for 'at least one' problems.
cards.storedExplanation: Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, |S| = 4. 'At least one head' = complement of 'no head' (= TT). P(no head) = 1/4. P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Direct count: HH, HT, TH all qualify → 3/4 ✓. The complementary trick (1 − P(none)) is invaluable for 'at least one' problems.

cards.front:
From a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards, a card is drawn at random. The probability of drawing a King OR a Heart is:

(A) 16/52
(B) 16/52 = 4/13
(C) 17/52
(D) 13/52
cards.back:
(B) 16/52 = 4/13

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Inclusion-Exclusion: P(K ∪ H) = P(K) + P(H) − P(K ∩ H). 4 Kings, 13 Hearts, 1 King-of-Hearts (counted in both). So 4 + 13 − 1 = 16 favourable cards. P = 16/52 = 4/13. Trap option 17/52 forgets to subtract the overlap (the King-of-Hearts).
cards.storedExplanation: Inclusion-Exclusion: P(K ∪ H) = P(K) + P(H) − P(K ∩ H). 4 Kings, 13 Hearts, 1 King-of-Hearts (counted in both). So 4 + 13 − 1 = 16 favourable cards. P = 16/52 = 4/13. Trap option 17/52 forgets to subtract the overlap (the King-of-Hearts).

cards.front:
Two fair dice are rolled. The probability that the sum of the numbers showing is 8 is:

(A) 5/36
(B) 1/6
(C) 1/9
(D) 7/36
cards.back:
(A) 5/36

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Sample space = 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes. Outcomes giving sum 8 — list them: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) → 5 outcomes. Probability = 5/36. Note: (4,4) is one outcome (not two, because two dice are independent and we're listing ordered pairs but the same pair). Common counts to memorise — sums 7 (=6/36, the most likely), 6 = 5/36, 8 = 5/36, 5 = 4/36, 9 = 4/36, 2 or 12 = 1/36 each.

cards.front:
A bag contains 5 white and 4 red balls. Two balls are drawn one after another WITHOUT replacement. The probability that BOTH are red is:

(A) 16/81
(B) 1/6
(C) 12/72
(D) 2/9
cards.back:
(B) 1/6

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Without replacement → conditional probability. P(1st red) = 4/9. After taking one red, 3 reds remain among 8 total. P(2nd red | 1st red) = 3/8. Joint probability = (4/9) × (3/8) = 12/72 = 1/6. With replacement, it would be (4/9)² = 16/81. Use the multiplication rule for sequential events; conditioning is the key word for 'without replacement'.

From 7 boys and 4 girls, a committee of 3 is to be formed. The probability that the committee has exactly 2 girls is:

(A) 21/55
(B) 42/165 = 14/55
(C) 21/165
(D) 1/3
cards.back:
(B) 42/165 = 14/55

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Total ways to pick 3 from 11: ¹¹C₃ = 165. Favourable = (pick 2 girls) × (pick 1 boy) = ⁴C₂ × ⁷C₁ = 6 × 7 = 42. Probability = 42/165 = 14/55. Verify by simplifying — divide by 3: 42/165 = 14/55 ≈ 0.2545. Check sum across all girl-counts: P(0G) + P(1G) + P(2G) + P(3G) = 35/165 + 84/165 + 42/165 + 4/165 = 165/165 = 1 ✓.

cards.front:
The sum of the first 20 natural numbers (1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 20) is:

(A) 200
(B) 210
(C) 220
(D) 190
cards.back:
(B) 210

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Sum of first n natural numbers: Sₙ = n(n+1)/2. For n = 20 → 20 × 21 / 2 = 210. Equivalently, AP sum: Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n−1)d] = 20/2 × [2 + 19] = 10 × 21 = 210. Sum of first n odd numbers = n². Sum of first n even numbers = n(n+1). Sum of squares = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Sum of cubes = [n(n+1)/2]² (interesting — square of the sum).

The sum of an infinite geometric progression with first term 1 and common ratio 1/2 is:

(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 1/2

cards.front:
If three numbers a, b, c are in AP (in that order), then 2b equals:

(A) ac
(B) a + c
(C) a − c
(D) a/c
cards.back:
(B) a + c

Algebra, Probability & Stats — Three numbers in AP: middle = average of outer two. So b = (a + c)/2 → 2b = a + c. Equivalently, b − a = c − b (common difference is the same on both sides). For GP, the analogous property: b² = ac (b is the GEOMETRIC MEAN of a and c). For HP (harmonic): 2/b = 1/a + 1/c. Useful for inserting means: between a and c, if we want 1 AM → b = (a+c)/2; 1 GM → b = √(ac); 1 HM → b = 2ac/(a+c). Always AM ≥ GM ≥ HM (with equality iff a = c).

(C) 8

cards.back:

Here a = 3, b = 5 → first term = 3 + 5 = 8; common difference = 2 × 3 = 6. Verify: S₁ = 3 + 5 = 8 → t₁ = 8. S₂ = 12 + 10 = 22 → t₂ = S₂ − S₁ = 22 − 8 = 14. d = t₂ − t₁ = 14 − 8 = 6 ✓.

cards.front:
Bar graph shows production: 2020=80, 2021=100, 2022=125, 2023=150 units. Compound growth rate from 2020 to 2023 is approximately:

(A) 23% per annum (using A=P(1+r)^3)
(B) 30% per annum (over-estimate)
(C) 70% over the 3-year period
(D) 20% just per year average
cards.back:
(A) 23% per annum (using A=P(1+r)^3)

Data Interpretation — Apply CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate): A = P(1+r)^n. Plug 150 = 80 × (1+r)^3 → (1+r)^3 = 1.875 → 1+r = (1.875)^(1/3) ≈ 1.234 → r ≈ 0.234 = 23.4%. RULE OF 72 CHECK: at 23%, doubling time = 72/23 ≈ 3.13 years; from 80 to 160 in ~3 years matches roughly (we got 150 in 3 years, so ~95% of doubled — close to expected). KEY DI METHOD: (1) GROWTH PROBLEMS — CAGR formula = ((end/start)^(1/years)) − 1. (2) CUMULATIVE GROWTH (over period) ≠ AVERAGE annual growth. (3) IMPORTANT — always specify: simple average vs CAGR. e.g., 70/3 = 23.3% simple average; CAGR is also ~23% here (close because growth is steady). EXAM PRACTICE: bar/line graphs commonly compare 4-5 years; common Q types: (a) % change between 2 specific years. (b) average growth rate. (c) which year saw highest/lowest value. (d) total over period. (e) ratio between two values. SHORTCUT: when dealing with growth rates near 10%, ratio (1.1)^3 ≈ 1.33; (1.2)^3 ≈ 1.73; (1.25)^3 ≈ 1.95 (~doubling in 3 years). PYQ FREQUENCY: bar-graph DI in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO Mains, CAT — 5+ Qs per paper.

RULE OF 72 CHECK: at 23%, doubling time = 72/23 ≈ 3.13 years; from 80 to 160 in ~3 years matches roughly (we got 150 in 3 years, so ~95% of doubled — close to expected). KEY DI METHOD: (1) GROWTH PROBLEMS — CAGR formula = ((end/start)^(1/years)) − 1. (2) CUMULATIVE GROWTH (over period) ≠ AVERAGE annual growth. (3) IMPORTANT — always specify: simple average vs CAGR. e.g., 70/3 = 23.3% simple average; CAGR is also ~23% here (close because growth is steady). EXAM PRACTICE: bar/line graphs commonly compare 4-5 years; common Q types: (a) % change between 2 specific years. (b) average growth rate. (c) which year saw highest/lowest value. (d) total over period. (e) ratio between two values. SHORTCUT: when dealing with growth rates near 10%, ratio (1.1)^3 ≈ 1.33; (1.2)^3 ≈ 1.73; (1.25)^3 ≈ 1.95 (~doubling in 3 years). PYQ FREQUENCY: bar-graph DI in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO Mains, CAT — 5+ Qs per paper.

cards.front:
Pie chart of 360°: subject A=72°, B=108°, C=90°, D=90°. If total marks = 1000, marks in B subject =?

(A) 300 marks (108/360 × 1000)
(B) 200 marks (an under-estimate)
(C) 250 marks (calc error here)
(D) 500 marks (over-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 300 marks (108/360 × 1000)

Data Interpretation — PIE CHART: total = 360°. SECTOR OF B = 108°. So B's share = 108/360 = 30%. Marks for B = 30% of 1000 = 300. SHORTCUT: pie chart degree to percent → divide by 3.6 (since 360/100 = 3.6). 108 ÷ 3.6 = 30. Same as 108/360 × 100. CHECK: A = 72/360 = 20% → 200 marks; B = 30% → 300; C = 90/360 = 25% → 250; D = 25% → 250. Sum = 200+300+250+250 = 1000 ✓. KEY PIE-CHART CONVERSIONS: (a) 18° = 5%; (b) 36° = 10%; (c) 72° = 20%; (d) 90° = 25%; (e) 108° = 30%; (f) 144° = 40%; (g) 180° = 50%; (h) 216° = 60%; (i) 252° = 70%; (j) 270° = 75%; (k) 360° = 100%. EXAM-FAVOURITE: pie-chart Qs typically ask: (1) value of a specific sector. (2) ratio of two sectors. (3) % difference between two sectors. (4) what was added/removed. PYQ FREQUENCY: pie chart in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Pre, IBPS PO Mains 5-10 DI Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests degree-to-percent intuition + careful percentage calculations.

cards.front:
Line graph: rainfall (mm) Jan=50, Feb=80, Mar=120, Apr=200, May=350, Jun=500. Average monthly rainfall is:

(A) About 217 mm (sum/6 calc)
(B) About 100 mm (under-estimate)
(C) About 350 mm (over-estimate)
(D) About 500 mm (max value)
cards.back:
(A) About 217 mm (sum/6 calc)

Data Interpretation — Sum = 50 + 80 + 120 + 200 + 350 + 500 = 1300. Number of months = 6. Average = 1300/6 ≈ 216.67 mm ≈ 217 mm. KEY METHOD: simple averaging of values. NUANCE — MEAN vs MEDIAN: (1) MEAN: 217 (computed). (2) MEDIAN: average of middle values (Mar=120, Apr=200) = 160. (3) MODE: not relevant here. INSIGHT: when data has OUTLIERS (here 500 is much higher than typical), MEAN is PULLED UP relative to MEDIAN. INDIA RAINFALL: SOUTHWEST MONSOON brings ~75% of annual rainfall in JUNE-SEPTEMBER. NORTHEAST MONSOON (Tamil Nadu, AP coast) — Oct-Dec. ANNUAL RAINFALL PATTERNS: (a) Mawsynram (Meghalaya) ~11,873 mm (highest in India). (b) Jaisalmer ~150 mm (lowest). PRACTICE — DI WITH MONSOON DATA: comparison of years, identifying drought years (typically <80% of long-term avg), heavy rainfall years (>110%). UPSC angle: agricultural geography + monsoon variability + climate change. PYQ FREQUENCY: line-graph DI in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B 5-10 DI Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests reading + arithmetic carefully under time pressure.

cards.front:
Table: Population A=4000, B=5000, C=6000. If A grew 10%, B fell 5%, C grew 20%, the new total is approximately:

(A) 16,350 (sum after percent changes)
(B) 15,000 (no change calc)
(C) 17,000 (over-estimate calc)
(D) 16,000 (under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 16,350 (sum after percent changes)

Data Interpretation — New A = 4000 × 1.10 = 4400. New B = 5000 × 0.95 = 4750. New C = 6000 × 1.20 = 7200. New total = 4400 + 4750 + 7200 = 16,350. SHORTCUT mental math: 10% of 4000 = 400 → +400 = 4400. 5% of 5000 = 250 → −250 = 4750. 20% of 6000 = 1200 → +1200 = 7200. Sum the values. KEY METHOD: when DI presents PERCENT-CHANGE data: (1) Compute NEW value for each item. (2) SUM them. ALTERNATIVE: (a) NET CHANGE = +400 − 250 + 1200 = +1350. (b) ORIGINAL TOTAL = 15000; NEW TOTAL = 15000 + 1350 = 16350. INSIGHT: faster to compute NET CHANGE (sum of plus/minus) and add to original total. SAMPLE COMMON DI scenarios: (a) Sales/revenue grew/fell by X% across products. (b) Population growth/decline. (c) Election votes change between elections. (d) Stock prices rise/fall in different sectors. PRACTICE: when a multi-segment data has different % changes, NEVER simply average the percentages — compute each segment then sum. PYQ FREQUENCY: complex DI calculations in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B Mains 5+ Qs per paper.

cards.front:
Mixed graph: Boys = 60% of total students (1000). Among boys, 40% wear glasses. Number of boys wearing glasses is:

(A) 240 (60% of 1000 × 40%)
(B) 400 (just 40% of total)
(C) 600 (just count of boys)
(D) 100 (way under-shot calc)
cards.back:
(A) 240 (60% of 1000 × 40%)

Data Interpretation — Step 1: TOTAL BOYS = 60% of 1000 = 600. Step 2: BOYS WEARING GLASSES = 40% of 600 = 240. KEY METHOD for nested percentages: APPLY PERCENTAGES SEQUENTIALLY (multiplicatively): 0.60 × 0.40 × 1000 = 0.24 × 1000 = 240. EXAM TRAP: compute 40% directly of 1000 → 400 (wrong; that's % of total, not % of boys). Or 60% × 40% = 24% of 1000 = 240 (correct). PRACTICE: GIRLS wearing glasses = 40% of girls = 0.4 × 400 = 160 (assuming 40% rate among girls). Total wearing glasses = 240 + 160 = 400. PERCENTAGE ratio: 400/1000 = 40% wear glasses overall (matches average). NESTED PERCENT problems are popular in DI: (a) breakdown by gender + opinion (favored/not). (b) by region + product. (c) by year + quarter. SAMPLE: 'In a survey, 60% are men; 30% of men prefer X; 70% of women prefer Y. What % of total prefer X?' — assume 1000 sample: men=600, men preferring X = 180; women=400; women NOT preferring Y = 30%, so 120 prefer X (assuming binary). Total preferring X = 180 + 120 = 300 = 30% of total. PYQ FREQUENCY: nested-percentage DI in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO Mains 1-2 per paper.

cards.front:
Caselet: Bank's total deposits = ₹500 crore. Savings 40%, Current 25%, Fixed 35%. If interest rates: Savings 4%, Current 0%, Fixed 7%, total interest payable per year is:

(A) ₹20.25 crore (weighted interest)
(B) ₹15 crore (under-estimate calc)
(C) ₹35 crore (over-estimate)
(D) ₹50 crore (way over-shot)
cards.back:
(A) ₹20.25 crore (weighted interest)

Data Interpretation — STEP-by-STEP: (1) Savings deposits = 40% of 500 = ₹200 crore × 4% = ₹8 crore interest. (2) Current = 25% of 500 = ₹125 crore × 0% = ₹0. (3) Fixed = 35% of 500 = ₹175 crore × 7% = ₹12.25 crore. TOTAL INTEREST = 8 + 0 + 12.25 = ₹20.25 crore. KEY METHOD for CASELETS: (1) READ entire passage carefully. (2) IDENTIFY the structure (multiple categories with rates). (3) COMPUTE for each category SEPARATELY. (4) SUM. CASELET DI is a DI subtype with TEXT description (not just visual chart) + multiple Qs. Common in IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B, banking exams. UPSC angle: financial inclusion + banking sector reforms (CAA-NRC, JAM trinity, GST, demonetization, etc.). KEY TERMS: (a) SAVINGS account — low interest, easy access. (b) CURRENT account — for businesses, no interest, unlimited transactions. (c) FIXED DEPOSIT (FD) — locked period, higher interest. (d) RECURRING DEPOSIT (RD) — regular monthly contribution. RBI POLICY RATE: REPO RATE — banks borrow from RBI; affects deposit + lending rates. As of April 2026: REPO ~5-6% (varies). PYQ FREQUENCY: bank-related DI in IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B Mains, SBI PO 5+ Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests financial-literacy + careful arithmetic.

CASELET: A company has 1,200 employees in total. 40 % are women. 30 % of the men and 25 % of the women are married. Q: How many UNMARRIED employees does the company have?

(A) 792
(B) 864
(C) 828
(D) 900
cards.back:
(B) 864

Data Interpretation — Women = 40 % × 1200 = 480. Men = 720. Married men = 30 % × 720 = 216. Married women = 25 % × 480 = 120. Total married = 336. Unmarried = 1200 − 336 = 864. Multi-step caselet item typical of Bank PO mains.
